entry.title: Prospects of reviving asset sale
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Prospects of reviving asset saleProspects of reviving asset sale

The disinvestment journey of the past decade has not been impressive. How it pans out now depends on some key factors

premium

Illustration: Binay SInha

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:35 PM ISTThe Narendra Modi government appears to be on a disinvestment drive. This is happening after a slow and halting implementation of its policy on strategic sale of public-sector undertakings (PSUs) it had announced in 2021.   Last week, the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to sell over 30 per cent of the government’s total equity in IDBI Bank at a price that should yield the central exchequer a disinvestment receipt of over ₹26,500 crore in the current year. With more than five months to go before the current year ends, the government will have collected more than its annual target of ₹80,000 crore from such asset sales during 2026-27. Equally important, the IDBI Bank deal means that the Modi government has now given a push to privatisation after a pause.  It is also important to note that the IDBI Bank privatisation doesn’t appear to be a flash in the pan. According to the finance ministry, the government plans to list three more PSUs on the stock exchange — India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd (IIFCL), Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd (MCL) and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd (SECL). Listing MCL and SECL may not result in any disinvestment receipts for the government, as they are wholly-owned subsidiaries of Coal India Ltd (CIL), which alone will benefit from such share sale proceeds. But the listing decision on IIFCL, wholly owned by the government, will mean more disinvestment receipt if it is listed before March 2027 as planned. Indeed, preparations for an initial public offer of IIFCL shares have already begun.   To be sure, the government’s track record on privatisation so far has been unimpressive. After formulating a policy on strategic disinvestment in 2021, wherein the government decided to exit all PSUs barring a few strategic ones, only Air India, Ferro Scrap Nigam, Neelachal Ispat Nigam and Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation have been privatised. Air India was a high-profile company, but owing to its huge, accumulated debt, the net proceeds for the government from its privatisation in January 2022 were only ₹2,700 crore.   Not that the sale of the other three companies saw higher realisation. The privatisation of Ferro Scrap and Neelachal Ispat yielded zero receipts. The sale proceed from Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation was ₹118.73 crore. That meant four cases of privatisation got the government only ₹2,818.73 crore. Critics of the government’s privatisation policy have not yet latched on to this number, but when they do, reservations about the policy on strategic sale of PSUs will only get more serious.   In the last twelve and a half years of the Modi government, total disinvestment receipts are estimated at ₹4.37 trillion, of which privatisation proceeds account for a tiny proportion of just 0.64 per cent, with the remaining amount being collected through the sale of minority shares. In the last one and a half years, asset monetisation (or the sale of land and buildings owned by government-owned PSUs) has picked up, with a total amount estimated at ₹34,787 crore. Even after including asset monetisation, total disinvestment proceeds in the Modi regime so far have been less than PSU dividend receipts of ₹5.32 trillion during this period.   This is perhaps one of the reasons for the government slowing down its disinvestment programme from 2021-22, ironically the same year when the government announced its policy on strategic sale of PSUs. It was argued by senior finance ministry functionaries then that value maximisation  was as important an objective in managing PSU assets as achieving disinvestment targets. This reflected a shift in strategy that was no longer overly dependent on strategic disinvestment and required a broader and more holistic approach decoupled from fiscal management.   Not surprisingly, the change in approach was visible in slowing disinvestment receipts, rising dividends from PSUs, and a sharp increase in the government’s equity contribution and loans released to PSUs in subsequent years. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, disinvestment receipts were estimated at just about 21 per cent of the total such proceeds during the twelve and a half years of the Modi government. In the same period, however, PSU dividends rose to ₹3.35 trillion, accounting for 63 per cent of total received by the government. And the government’s equity and loans to PSUs in this period rose to ₹21.45 trillion, over 57 per cent of what was allocated from 2021-22 to 2026-27. It was during the same period that the government’s Budget documents stopped referring to disinvestment in its capital receipts calculations. In what seemed to be part of its plan to de-emphasise disinvestment, all receipts from asset sales were classified as non-debt capital receipts.    Now that the government’s approach to disinvestment is changing, it will be important to keep track of a few parameters of the government’s receipts and expenditure allocations. One, it will be helpful if disinvestment receipts and asset monetisation receipts are clearly identified in the receipts budget, so that these numbers can be easily identified and subjected to analysis and dissemination.  Two, tracking disinvestment numbers will be important. But equally important will be the need to measure the pace at which the government is investing in PSUs through equity contribution and loans. In the early years of the Modi government, the amount allocated for equity and loans to PSUs was a little more than a third of the government’s total capital expenditure budget. In the last few years, this share has been close to 50 per cent. This trend should be reversed without any decline in the government’s overall capex target.   Three, it will be necessary to keep a close watch on the ratio between the government’s total receipts from PSUs (through disinvestment and dividend income) and the amount it spends on them through equity and loans. In the last five years, the amount of government receipts from PSUs as a share of total spending on PSUs has steadily fallen from around 30 per cent in 2021-22 to 15 per cent in 2024-25, before recovering a bit to about 26 per cent in 2025-26. This ratio should get better over time as the government’s disinvestment receipts increase and the need for fresh equity infusion declines.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Not in default, but already affected
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Not in default, but already affectedNot in default, but already affected

Evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects

premium

In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework

Aaraadhya SrivastavaPratibha KumariJithin P5 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTThe Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), a landmark reform introduced during the first term of the Modi government, marked its 10th anniversary in May 2026. Commentaries assessing the IBC’s performance have critiqued it on three grounds: (1) delays in the resolution process, (2) the relatively large share of concluded cases ending in liquidation rather than restructuring, and (3) the large haircuts suffered by creditors.  These are valid concerns regarding the functioning of the IBC once a firm enters insolvency proceedings. However, these very features determine what lenders expect to recover upon default and, consequently, shape the terms on which they extend credit before any default occurs. Thus, evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects. We, therefore, look beyond the insolvency process to examine how the reform affected firms that never entered insolvency proceedings.  In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework. Before the IBC, creditors recovered barely a quarter of the value of distressed assets, while resolution often took more than four years, according to the World Bank’s Doing Business 2015 report. By 2020, recovery rates under the IBC had risen to over 45 per cent, while average resolution time had fallen to around 413 days, a remarkable turnaround from the multi-year delays of the past. This early period provides a useful setting for understanding the effects of improvements in the insolvency resolution process, before subsequent challenges weakened these gains.  Quicker resolution reduced the deadweight costs associated with lengthy bankruptcy proceedings, while higher recovery rates strengthened lenders’ confidence in the enforceability of their claims. With lower expected losses in the event of default, lenders had greater incentives to expand the supply of credit and lend at a lower cost than before. Research supports this argument.In a 2021 paper published in the Journal of Corporate Finance, Bose, Filomeni, and Mallick document that the IBC expanded the availability of low-cost credit to distressed firms.  Distressed firms, in turn, had an incentive to use their additional borrowing capacity to finance risky projects. Why? Because if such projects succeeded, the resulting improvement in cash flows could allow firms to avoid default. Consistent with this possibility, Singh, Chauhan, and Jadiyappa (2022), in a paper published in Finance Research Letters, document that the IBC induced distressed firms to take on more risk than non-distressed firms, with the increase in risk-taking accompanied by improved operating performance. These results suggest that a bankruptcy law that rapidly resolves insolvency, as the IBC did during its initial years, can both enable creditors to recover a larger fraction of their dues more quickly and improve the prospects of distressed firms.  These findings should not, however, imply that the IBC mattered only for distressed firms. The reform could also have affected the financing and investment decisions of relatively healthy firms. How? By improving expected recovery for lenders and making the insolvency process more time-bound, the IBC may have increased the amount of credit that lenders were willing to extend against a given pool of collateral. Firms with a greater stock of collateralisable assets could then have accessed additional debt to finance value-enhancing activities such as capital-goods imports, which can serve as a source of technological upgrading. We tested this hypothesis and found that, following the introduction of the IBC, import-dependent firms with more pledgeable assets borrowed more and used the additional funds to increase their capital-goods imports by about 31 per cent relative to otherwise comparable firms.  Put together, these findings suggest that the IBC has consequences even for firms that never enter insolvency. Its influence, however, depends on lenders perceiving it as a credible mechanism for timely recovery. Recent evidence of prolonged insolvency proceedings raises concerns in this regard. According to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India newsletter for the April-June 2026 quarter, the average time taken to complete a restructuring process was 1,026 days, while the average liquidation process took 1,378 days. Such delays may undermine lenders’ confidence in the framework, with implications for the supply and cost of credit. Weaker confidence could, in turn, affect firms’ access to external finance, constrain investment by viable firms, and increase the likelihood of default among financially weaker firms.  The IBC should, therefore, be judged not only by what happens when firms default, but also by how the prospect of default shapes the behaviour of firms and lenders before it occurs. Its greatest contribution may lie not in resolving insolvency after the fact, but in changing behaviour before it does. For that to happen, however, the promise of timely resolution must remain credible.
The writers are, respectively,  assistant professor at the Indian Institute of Management, Ranchi;assistant professor at TAPMI, Bengaluru; and assistant professor at the Indian Institute of Management, Raipur. entry.title: Confronting economic trade-offs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Confronting economic trade-offsConfronting economic trade-offs

Market-driven prices and tax reforms can support monetary policy and attract foreign capital

premium

Rising bond yields, rupee depreciation and uncertain foreign capital flows have renewed the debate over monetary policy, market-driven interest rates and tax reforms in India. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ananth Narayan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 12:04 AM ISTIn a difficult global environment, interest rates have risen, the rupee has weakened, and net foreign-capital flows remain uncertain. It is worth looking at the takeaways from the recent past to consider the road ahead.  What happened? With consumer inflation averaging just 2 per cent in 2025, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) cut the policy repo rate by 125 basis points (bps) to 5.25 per cent. In financial year (FY) 2025-26, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also bought government bonds worth 2.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) to support growth and replenish liquidity drained by foreign exchange outflows. These record RBI bond purchases were 70 per cent higher than those in 2020-21, during the Covid pandemic, and were 85 per cent of the Centre’s net borrowing in FY26.  Indian bond yields consequently fell. The difference between India and US 10-year bond yields declined to multi-decade lows of below 2 percentage points. Given that the difference between inflation in India and the US also narrowed, this may seem reasonable. However, rates should be determined by demand and supply from willing borrowers and lenders. In India, the lender pushing down interest rates was the RBI, not willing savers. For discretionary savers, post-tax returns on fixed-income remained unattractive.  Repressing interest rates so forcefully has consequences. Discretionary savings shifted away from fixed-income investments to equities, contributing to pockets of overvaluation there. Net foreign-inflows struggled, partly due to these high equity valuations. Outward direct investments also rose. Narrower rate differentials compressed dollar-rupee forward premia, making hedging and speculation against the rupee cheaper.  Across FY25 and FY26, the RBI net sold $192 billion in currency markets, much of it to feed hedging and speculative dollar demand. As dollar outflows drained rupee liquidity, markets signalled the need for higher interest rates. Instead, the RBI’s bond purchases and other actions poured durable liquidity into a leaky bucket. Short-term instruments could have replenished liquidity without depressing long-term yields.  The rupee fell from 85 per dollar in January 2025 to 92.5 by mid-February 2026, before the Iran conflict took it towards 97. We sought low rates, currency stability, and capital inflows. Yet despite many large market interventions, subsidised foreign exchange (FX) swaps, and restrictions on currency trading, pressures persist.  Lessons for stakeholders:  Armchair advice, present company included, is easy to dispense. With that acknowledged, three lessons stand out.  First, as the last few years have demonstrated, the impossible trinity matters. Monetary independence, capital mobility and exchange-rate stability involve inevitable trade-offs. The 2014 Urjit Patel Committee recognised this, prioritising inflation control at the time while envisaging greater flexibility once inflation expectations were anchored. Yet the RBI’s August 2025 monetary framework review did not even mention this trilemma.  Second, clear communication about policy choices and trade-offs is essential for market confidence. Pursuing multiple, conflicting objectives simultaneously while avoiding trade-offs risks undermining credibility. We could then end up with the worst of all worlds.  Third, large interventions in interconnected markets risk unintended consequences. Consistency also requires reframing the debate from “let the rupee find its own level” to “let both the rupee and rupee interest rates find their own levels”.  The way forward: Allow market-determined rates. Rather than repressing interest rates with interventions and schemes, we should largely let discretionary savings fund borrowings. Free debt markets should also allow for freer and more stable currency markets.  To be fair, in FY27, the RBI has net sold ₹1.25 trillion of government bonds to absorb liquidity created by its FX swap scheme. The MPC raised the repo rate by 25 bps this month. Yet the current India-US 10-year bond yield spread is at 230 bps, well below its historical median of around 400 bps. It is unclear if this will attract savings into Indian debt.  For credibility, the MPC and RBI must demonstrate the same willingness to tighten monetary conditions as they showed in easing them. Moving banking liquidity towards neutral would give market forces greater scope to determine bond yields.  What about growth?  Higher interest rates can impact growth. However, a lower tax burden on fixed-income can allow for lower headline rates. Interest and some fixed-income capital gains are taxed at marginal income-tax rates, leaving savers with unattractive post-tax returns.  We could tax interest income, including from fixed deposits, at the lower of, say, 20 per cent or the applicable slab rate. Capital gains on debt funds could be taxed on a par with equities.  This would also let risk-return considerations, rather than taxation, drive savings allocation. Tax revenue losses may also be limited, since tax-sensitive savers likely avoid direct fixed-income already.  Remove impediments to foreign portfolio flows:   India is an outlier in taxing capital gains earned by foreign investors on non-controlling portfolio investments in equities and corporate bonds. Most countries allow such gains to be taxed where the investor resides. Indian tax residents investing in overseas securities largely pay capital gains tax only in India.  Residence-based taxation is, therefore, not a discriminatory tax exemption only for foreigners. Their gains remain subject to tax rules in their home countries. Tax treaties do not fully address this irritant. Many foreign investors cannot offset Indian taxes against their home taxes. They may also pay Indian tax on rupee gains even when their dollar returns are poor. Compliance adds further to costs and complexity.  India’s June 2026 tax relief for qualifying foreign investment in government securities offers a useful precedent. Extending such residence-based taxation to corporate bonds and equities would significantly ease foreign investment. An increase in the securities transaction tax for foreign investors, particularly on high-turnover derivatives, could offset the resulting loss in tax revenue. These reforms cannot guarantee foreign inflows in an uncertain world. But they would remove distortions and allow for more palatable policy trade-offs.  Strengthen tax policy consultation:  Capital-market tax reforms deserve comprehensive consultation, akin to the ones that regulators undertake.  This can bring in expertise and clarity and enhance policy credibility. India retains meaningful buffers and macroeconomic strength. Credible policies, backed by clear communication that confronts difficult trade-offs, will help us navigate these uncertain times.

entry.title: RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?

As the central bank announces a new set of bold regulatory measure, this question is worth asking

premium

The RBI's latest forex regulations have raised concerns over higher currency hedging costs and their potential impact on investment and the rupee | Representative Picture

Rajeswari Sengupta5 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 10:16 PM ISTWhen the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR (B), scheme in June 2026 to attract dollar inflows, many saw it as a turning point in the battle to stabilise the rupee. A few of us were sceptical. Now, the RBI has announced a new set of bold regulatory measures. Should we be sceptical again?  Understanding the past is key to ascertaining the future. So, let’s review. The RBI ended the FCNR(B) scheme on August 31, a month earlier than planned, suggesting that the $133 billion that the scheme had attracted was more than sufficient. Yet on October 10, the RBI tightened foreign exchange regulations significantly, including imposing a hefty tax on forward purchases of dollars. Naturally, people are asking: Why were these measures necessary if the FCNR(B) scheme was hailed as a success?  The answer is not clear. The RBI has mentioned the need to preserve financial stability, but surely the Indian financial system is not in any danger. In the absence of a clear official explanation, the public is left to figure out what problem these measures are meant to address, whether they will succeed or whether their benefits will outweigh the costs to the economy. Let’s try to address these questions.  There are two possible explanations for why the rupee has been depreciating for such a long time: Sentiment towards the Indian economy has soured or India’s balance of payments (BoP) is suffering from structural shocks.  Consider the case where the problem is merely one of sentiment. In that case, it may be reasonable to think that strong measures could jolt the market back to its senses.  Reasonable, but wrong. We know this because that strategy has already been tried and it didn’t work. Despite the huge FCNR (B) inflows, the RBI has continued to actively intervene in the foreign exchange markets and, according to some estimates, it has already used up nearly half the dollar inflows mobilised through various concessional swap schemes introduced since June 2026, including the FCNR(B) scheme. Yet the rupee has continued to depreciate. And it now seems that these schemes were not enough, which is why the RBI has resorted to regulatory interventions.  This suggests that the rupee’s decline may not merely be a problem of worsening sentiment; it could be a structural story. In fact, over the last couple of years, India has been hit by a series of macroeconomic shocks, such as falling behind in the development of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models and the West Asia war, which has imposed a huge energy bill on the country. Perhaps the most disappointing has been the realisation that “China+1” did not translate into a shift of global manufacturing to India, as can be seen from the low levels of foreign direct investment.  If these are indeed the underlying factors responsible for the rupee’s persistent decline, then yet another round of palliative measures will, at best, provide short-term relief. It is true that palliatives can at times be useful, as a way to buy time until more fundamental cures are implemented. However, the problem in this case is that the benefits of the recent measures are likely to be small, and will be exceeded by their costs.  First, the sudden imposition of such stringent measures so soon after the “successful” June 2026 schemes, suggests to the market that the RBI is deeply worried about India’s BoP prospects. It signals that the RBI has concluded that conditions are so fragile that conventional interventions in the spot and forward markets are no longer enough to manage currency volatility. It is then natural for foreign investors to worry as well. In other words, rather than restoring confidence, the RBI’s new measures risk reinforcing the very pessimism they are meant to address.  Second, the new measures have already resulted in a big jump in currency hedging costs. According to some reports, the one-year forward premium has risen above 4.5 per cent, its highest level since January 2022. For importers, exporters or investors using forward contracts to buy or sell dollars in the future, a higher forward premium means it becomes more expensive to hedge currency risk. This is particularly costly for Indian manufacturers, many of whom depend heavily on imported inputs. As hedging becomes more expensive, they will now be forced to bear greater currency risk themselves. This uncertainty can further discourage them from investing, the exact opposite of what the economy needs.  In the end, the latest measures announced by the RBI are unlikely to stem the rupee’s decline, but they risk imposing further costs on an economy where underlying growth momentum remains weak. This brings us back to the central question: What prompted the RBI to take such drastic steps? It is important for the central bank to explain the rationale behind its decision and how it expects the benefits to outweigh the costs.

entry.title: Let the people hedge
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Let the people hedgeLet the people hedge

Recent measures have gone beyond merely curbing speculation in the foreign-exchange market policy rules 

premium

The RBI's measures to defend the rupee have pushed up currency hedging costs, raising concerns over their impact on importers, exporters and India's foreign-exchange market. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Mihir S Sharma6 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 12:44 AM ISTThere are many questions about the rupee to which one never seems to get straight answers. The first one — often asked by foreign investors when told of India’s economic outperformance – is: If growth is going so well and macroeconomic fundamentals are strong, why is the rupee constantly sinking How has it lost 11 per cent against the dollar since May last year, worse than most of its emerging-market peers  There may be some reasonable answers to that — for example, that the same foreign investors are partly responsible, in that they’re pulling money out at record rates. Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn over ₹3 trillion from Indian equities so far this year. That’s already 1.8 times the amount they took out in all of 2025. And it appears to be accelerating; September was a six-month high with net withdrawals of ₹0.35 trillion, and the same number for the first 11 days of October was already ₹0.44 trillion.  But another question is far harder to answer: Why, precisely, can’t we let the rupee depreciate Once again, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) feels called upon to defend the currency against “speculation”. This rarely makes sense, particularly as the sight of a central bank mounting a defence attracts actual speculators the same way as blood in the water attracts sharks. Anything that looks like an implicit peg is a particularly bad idea. Speculators can usually view such a thing as an easy asymmetric bet — a licence to print money. Central banks should go out of their way to avoid giving traders any such impression. The RBI, however, seems to have forgotten this rule: It is being generally reported that many believe it has set a floor for the rupee-dollar exchange rate at ₹97 to the dollar.  Reuters has reported that traders estimate the central bank has already deployed $75 billion-80 billion on this defence, through spot sales and swaps, over the past four months. There may be no shortage of dollars in the RBI’s coffers at the moment – particularly given the inflow of $133 billion through the foreign-currency non-resident deposit scheme took reserves to a record high in September — but $75 billion is nevertheless a lot of money.  It is possible that the central bank genuinely believes that all this is transitory, and that the rupee is undervalued. Certainly, the governor has himself said in the past fortnight that this might be true, judging against measures like the six-currency real effective exchange rate (Reer). Analysts from HDFC Mutual Fund agree, saying that Reer has fallen to 10 per cent below its 10-year average, a mark last seen during the 2013 “taper tantrum”.  So what we’re being told is that markets are irrational. Fine, sometimes they are. But that’s not a good enough reason to fight them. Individual investors often have to be reminded that the market can stay irrational longer than they can remain solvent. That does not apply to central banks, perhaps. But even they might find that markets can stay wrong after they’ve deployed all their firepower.  Let’s look at what’s already been done. The non-resident Indians’ bank-deposit scheme was one effort to reduce pressure on the rupee. That made up for some of the hits the RBI took in late March and early April, when it intervened both by selling dollars and by using offshore derivatives. It restricted banks using the onshore forward market; capped net open positions; and later, it cracked down on non-deliverable forwards. By October, it had also raised rates and started tightening liquidity.  In each case, the positive effect on the rupee’s value has largely been transient, while the negative effect of heavy-handed regulation may last longer. Certainly, that’s what seems to be the case when one looks at the cost of hedging against a weaker rupee. The three-month yield on onshore dollar-rupee forwards — how much extra you have to pay to secure dollars against delivery three months ahead — reached 6.54 per cent. (The same measure was 1.09 per cent in November 2023.)  That came after the latest, most sweeping measures from the RBI, which attempted to detach the oil-marketing companies’ dollar demands from the broader market, as well as various other controls on derivatives, including requiring authorised dealers to keep cash with the central bank worth 20 per cent of each high-value derivative contract. Global macro analysts compare this to the tools that the People’s Bank of China uses to manage the yuan. Research by IDFC First Bank suggested this new reserve requirement might itself raise hedging costs by about 1.5 per cent.  This will hit not just importers, who will find themselves more exposed to further rupee depreciation – indeed, some reports emerged that banks were simply refusing to sign contracts with smaller companies and shut down online portals that did so — but perhaps also exporters with thin margins such as those in the readymade garments business. Leaving exposure unhedged naturally increases financial vulnerability all round.  It is too soon to declare that what we have seen over the past few months is a major reversal of India’s decades-long trend towards liberalising the foreign-exchange market. But market participants are saying quite openly that it is. That should worry us, because such perceptions are self-reinforcing.  And, at the end of the day, the reason that there is demand to hedge against a falling rupee is because most people believe that the currency has further to fall. Denying them the opportunity to hedge will not change their beliefs in any way. And beliefs are what determine market prices, including exchange rates.  A depreciating rupee is not in itself something that should terrify us. Why does it continue to sink Well, because of the real fundamentals of the Indian economy: It imports too much and does not export enough. You can plug this gap for a while with capital inflows; but, eventually, those may reverse. Then you can try to use reserves or regulation. But none of that changes the fundamental supply and demand equation. Seeing this imbalance, the market attempts to address it by making imports more expensive, so we buy less of them, and making our exports cheaper, so foreigners buy more of them. Fighting this natural process is neither effective nor in the long-term national interests.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: RBI supplements financial muscle with regulatory heft
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI supplements financial muscle with regulatory heftRBI supplements financial muscle with regulatory heft

Measures to curb dollar demand have strengthened the rupee, but raise costs for importers and leave the durability of the recovery uncertain

premium

The RBI’s forex curbs have supported the rupee but raised hedging costs for importers amid persistent pressure on the currency.

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 11:18 PM ISTLast week, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sent a strong message that it will change the rules of the game in the foreign exchange (forex) markets anytime by, besides other measures, imposing heavy costs for forward purchases of foreign currency by importers. The sledgehammer blow strengthened the rupee from nearly 97 to 95 against the US dollar but left unhedged exporters gaping at lower realisations in rupees than they estimated and importers staring at payments against forward contracts higher than prevailing spot rates.   The RBI says that its policy is not to target any exchange rate but to curb excessive volatility in the forex markets. Its actions suggest concern about the level too. On May 20 this year, the rupee depreciated to almost 97 to a US dollar, before recovering in subsequent days. To augment the supply of foreign currency, the RBI introduced, in early June, concessional swap facilities against Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B), deposits, banks’ overseas foreign currency borrowings and public sector external commercial borrowings. Although about $143.6 billion was mobilised under these facilities, expectations of further rupee depreciation could not be quelled. Crude oil prices and foreign investors’ withdrawals continued to put pressure on the rupee. Importers continued to book their exposures forward and many exporters left their positions open. RBI regularly sold foreign currency to support the rupee. Its reserves fell from $785.706 billion on September 4 to $726.027 billion on October 9, although valuation changes also affected the reserves. On October 9, the rupee closed at 96.73.  The RBI decided to act, this time by curbing demand for foreign currency. It provided a dollar window for public sector oil companies, tightened documentation, prohibited rebooking cancelled rupee derivative contracts and introduced the Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), requiring banks to maintain non-interest-bearing cash equal to 20 per cent of qualifying contracts’ rupee notional value. That raised costs for importers booking new hedges. Those holding existing forward contracts could roll them over but not cancel and rebook them to take advantage of lower rates.   The rupee closed at 94.96 on Friday, gaining nearly two per cent during the week. The RBI clarified that market-making and proprietary transactions are excluded from FERR. That reduced uncertainty but did not remove the additional cost of qualifying hedges.  The domestic forex turnover has nearly doubled from $41 billion daily in FY22 to about $80 billion. Outstanding rupee derivatives have increased nearly fourfold since FY21 to about ₹130 trillion. The daily rupee trading worldwide increased from $119 billion in 2022 to $185 billion in 2025. These figures do not represent equivalent net demand for dollars but demonstrate the expanding scale and international reach of the market in which RBI intervenes. Selling dollars can relieve immediate pressure; countering persistent expectations of depreciation can require repeated drawdown of reserves. The recent measures suggest that RBI sought to supplement its financial firepower with regulatory power, changing the costs and conditions of transactions to restrain dollar demand.  The recent measures make protection more expensive for genuine importers. Whether the costs imposed on trade are justified by the gains and whether they will sustain the recovery remain uncertain. The structural factors that cause the weakening of the rupee have not gone away.   The traders should remain cautious, always remembering that RBI has its own priorities.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Fragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Fragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growthFragmented rules, missing incentives hold back India's green finance growth

A unified green taxonomy, standardised legal documentation, and tangible economic incentives are urgently needed

premium

green finance, India green finance market, green taxonomy, RBI, Sebi, sustainable finance, green bonds, ESG, green deposits, climate finance, green lending, NBFCs, green debt securities, SNG Partners

Rajesh Narain Gupta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 11:02 PM ISTThe devastating floods that swept through Nepal in August 2026 did more than displace communities and disrupt cross-border trade. They served as a stark reminder that climate risk is no longer a distant, abstract concern, but a reality at India’s doorstep. Events of this magnitude necessitate a hard look at how we are funding our climate response.  Over the last decade, sustainable finance has moved into the mainstream of global capital markets. Green bonds, green deposits; and environmental, social, and governance (ESG)-labelled loans are now supported by thick layers of regulation and third-party verification. Yet, India’s share of the global green finance market remains an underwhelming one per cent. In stark contrast, the European Union (EU) dominates with a 45 per cent share, having successfully created an ecosystem that attracts robust private capital.  The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued climate-finance directions for banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), while the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) regulates green debt securities. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has also pushed for greater transparency through its business responsibility and sustainability reporting framework. However, the intent is often overshadowed by the implementation, which has unwittingly become a deterrent for market participants.  A key challenge stunting India’s green finance is a fragmented regulatory landscape. Regulators are operating through disparate rules and supervisory expectations rather than a cohesive policy framework. The most glaring gap is the absence of a finalised, statutory national green taxonomy. While the European Union’s taxonomy provides a uniform set of criteria to determine sustainable activities, India continues to rely on interim lists.  This absence of an anchor taxonomy forces issuers to seek bespoke legal opinions on eligibility for every green issue. It also creates a gap in documentation, as definitions linked to an official taxonomy are missing. The regulatory architecture demands extensive upfront disclosures, ongoing post-listing updates, and third-party impact reporting. Without Sebi or RBI-approved model documents or standard loan clauses, drafting these regulatory obligations into transaction documents is time-consuming and inconsistent. For smaller issuers, this multiplies legal review costs and acts as a severe barrier to entry.  To fix this, India needs scaled disclosures. The rules currently apply uniformly to all issuers regardless of size. Exploring a reduced pre-listing and post-listing disclosure regime for smaller issuances could heavily incentivise participation. Standardised template covenants for green financing would also ensure greater efficiency and enable quicker legal sign-offs.  Another major bottleneck is the lack of fiscal or prudential carrots. It is a common misconception that regulatory frameworks inherently offer financial perks for green initiatives. In reality, the RBI has not built prudential concessions into its climate finance directions. There are no relaxations on the cash reserve ratio (CRR) or statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) for green lending.  Green deposits are placed on the exact same commercial footing as ordinary rupee term deposits. Because current regulations expressly forbid a differential interest rate, there is no tangible “greenium” to attract depositors or lower the cost of capital for borrowers. ESG ratings are also not yet a mandatory input into credit decisions for banks in India; a higher ESG rating does not automatically equate to a lower cost of capital. Therefore, the pricing incentive for a borrower with strong environmental credentials currently lives in loan documentation rather than systemic regulation.  Permitting differential interest rates on green deposits would encourage both investors and borrowers to participate in the green debt market. Furthermore, the introduction of dedicated green alternative investment funds (AIFs) under the current Sebi regime would ensure a disciplined approach to the green use of proceeds.  India has successfully laid the foundation for a sustainable finance ecosystem. However, the next leap requires moving away from overlapping regulations towards regulatory harmonisation. A unified green taxonomy, standardised legal documentation, and tangible economic incentives are urgently needed. A well-intentioned regulatory framework without matching financial rewards is like an engine without fuel. If India wants to secure its position in the global green finance landscape, it must ensure the rules actually encourage the market to move. ______________________________________________________________________________________________________  The writer is founder & chairman, SNG Partners, Advocates & Solicitors   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessonsAT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons

The Supreme Court's ruling on Yes Bank's AT-1 bond write-off raises concerns over RBI oversight, financial product mis-selling and the limitations of disclosure-based regulation.

premium

The Supreme Court's ruling on Yes Bank's ₹8,415 crore AT-1 bond write-off has renewed scrutiny of regulatory oversight, investor protection and the mis-selling of complex financial products.

Debashis Basu5 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:56 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has finally drawn a line under one of the most disturbing episodes in India’s recent banking history. On October 15, it dismissed appeals by Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and the Union government against the Bombay High Court’s 2023 decision to set aside the writeoff of ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank’s Additional Tier 1 (AT-1) bonds. The issue before the court was whether the authorities had proceeded lawfully in imposing these losses. The court held that the administrator appointed to run Yes Bank had no authority to extinguish the bonds after the final reconstruction scheme came into force. Beyond these legal technicalities, the AT-1 saga throws up two bigger questions: First, the conduct of the RBI as regulator; and second, the entire regulatory philosophy of “disclosure-based regulation”.  

RBI as a “bystander”

Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds were actively sold to individuals even though the regulatory framework treated them as sophisticated, high-risk securities. This was not merely a case of investors buying something risky and subsequently complaining when the risk materialised. In April 2021, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), not the RBI, completed its investigation into Yes Bank’s gross mis-selling of AT-1 bonds. The findings were devastating. Customers were told that the bonds were effectively “Super FDs”, offering a 9 per cent-plus return with the appearance of fixed-deposit (FD) safety. In several cases, the term sheet was not supplied, and customers were not given adequate confirmation that they understood the product’s features and risks. Sebi said some customers were persuaded to shift money from fixed deposits to these risky securities.  The Supreme Court has called the conduct of Yes Bank, the RBI, and the administrator “questionable”, and said that putting investors at the receiving end of administrative lapses would be “highly unfair”. It specifically said that tighter scrutiny should have been exercised before individual investors were lured into these securities. The court described the RBI as a “mere bystander” in the whole saga. The data placed before the Supreme Court identified 1,346 retail investors with around ₹679 crore invested in Yes Bank’s AT1 bonds. Of these, 1,311 were the bank’s existing customers, with nearly ₹663 crore invested. Sebi found that Yes Bank had failed to ensure that investors understood the risks. It penalised Yes Bank and its executives for the mis-selling, including a ₹25 crore penalty on the bank and a ₹2 crore penalty on then chief executive officer Rana Kapoor. Despite these startling facts, the RBI continued to defend the writeoff.  

Disclosure-based regulation

 There is an even bigger issue here. When India liberalised its financial sector, it embraced what is called “disclosure-based regulation”. The philosophy is that the regulator will frame the rules, including disclosure requirements; the seller will provide them along with the product; and investors, acting intelligently and rationally, will decide for themselves what is good for them.  This concept owes something to the old principle of caveat emptor, or “buyer beware”, which was common in an unregulated world of commercial transactions. If an investor buys a risky product after being told about the risks, the consequences are supposedly the investor’s responsibility. This sounds reasonable until one looks at how financial regulation actually works. Regulators do not merely ask financial institutions to disclose information. They make extraordinarily detailed rules about products, capital, eligibility, distribution, advertising, risk profiling, suitability, documentation, sales practices, compensation, and reporting. They specify what banks and financial intermediaries can and cannot do. They issue circulars, master directions, frequently asked questions (FAQs), clarifications, and enforcement orders. The regulatory state is anything but laissez-faire, the environment in which caveat emptor made sense.  The regulator is sufficiently interventionist to write detailed rules, but then retreats into a hands-off posture to say that investors must bear the consequences when those rules fail to protect them. This creates an extraordinarily convenient arrangement for private interests. The gains from selling complex financial products are privatised; the consequences of bad sales practices are pushed on to investors; and regulatory failure is discovered only after the damage has been done. Like Yes Bank’s AT-1 bonds, AAA-rated bonds of Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd (IL&FS) had been wrongly sold, while mis-selling life insurance to senior citizens is an everyday affair.  If AT-1 bonds were so complex and risky that the regulatory framework specified the categories of investors to whom they could be offered, why should disclosure to an inappropriate investor cure the problem? There is a fundamental information and power asymmetry between a financial-services company and an ordinary customer. The former employs lawyers, accountants, investment bankers, risk managers, and compliance officers. It designs the product, determines the sales pitch, trains its employees, and controls the information presented to the customer. The individual investor does none of these things. To pretend that the two parties become equal merely because a disclosure document has been handed over is to confuse formal consent with informed consent.  It is time to confront the hypocrisy of “disclosure-based regulation” and move towards outcome-based regulation. This would mean asking whether the product is suitable for the customer; whether the seller has an incentive to mis-sell it; whether the customer has the capacity to understand it; whether the institution is complying with the rules; and whether the regulator is actually watching. Today, the answer to all five questions is effectively: The investor was warned. This should change.

entry.title: King Canute and the sea waves
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / King Canute and the sea wavesKing Canute and the sea waves

Let the rupee find its own level but allow that to happen in a calibrated way

premium

After touching almost 97 to the dollar on October 9, the rupee has bounced back to 94.96 on October 16. Will the trend continue? Is there anything else the RBI can do? | Image: Bloomberg

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:38 PM ISTThis is an apocryphal story. King Canute, the 11th-century Anglo-Scandinavian king, had his throne carried down to the seashore at tide. Sitting before the incoming ocean, he commanded the waves to recede so his royal robes did not get wet. The sea ignored him and washed over his feet.  Now imagine the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as King Canute and the currency market as the sea.  Early last week, less than a week after the October monetary policy, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra told Moneycontrol that the central bank would do whatever it took to ensure orderly movement in the forex market.  On the same day, speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the central bank's priority was to ensure orderly market conditions rather than defend a specific exchange rate. Her statement came days after the RBI unveiled yet another package of measures to calm the currency market.  In his post-monetary policy media interaction on October 7, Malhotra said: “By a number of estimates, including the REER, the rupee is not overvalued; it may be undervalued.” He also referred to the RBI’s dollar selling (in the context of how liquidity is being drained). REER is Real Effective Exchange Rate which measures the strength of a country's currency against a weighted basket of its major trading partners' currencies, adjusted for inflation.  What has the RBI done so far to ensure orderly market conditions or stop rupee depreciation? It depends on the prism we are looking through. But before that, here’s a quick recap of the history of rupee depreciation and RBI actions.  In 1997-98, during the East Asian financial crisis, the rupee depreciated roughly 10-12 per cent, sliding from 35.7 a dollar in mid-1997 to 39-40 by early 1998. India’s foreign exchange reserves were a modest $26-29 billion at that time.  The RBI tightened monetary policy by raising the rate and cash reserve ratio (CRR). Subsequently, it raised at least $4.23 billion through Resurgent India Bonds in August 1998 to shore up reserve buffers following the US post-Pokhran sanctions, and another $5.5 billion through India Millennium Deposits in October-November 2000 to counter capital flight during the global tech stock crash.  In 2008–2009, the rupee dropped 25-30 per cent, from 39-40 a dollar in early 2008 to 51-52 by early 2009 during the global financial crisis. Forex reserves dropped from a peak of $316 billion to $250 billion due to heavy market interventions and capital flight by foreign institutional investors (FIIs).  Besides aggressive dollar-selling in spot and forward markets, the RBI pursued an easy money policy, cutting the rate, CRR, and the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR). The global financial crisis prompted monetary easing. The RBI also opened special forex swap facilities for oil marketing companies.  In 2013, during the taper tantrum, the rupee quickly depreciated by nearly 20-25 per cent, falling from 54 a dollar to a then-record low of near 68.8 in August while forex reserves dropped by $30 billion to $270 billion.  The RBI’s response was to open the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) – FCNR(B) – swap scheme (September-November 2013), attracting $34.3 billion in foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians by subsidising swap costs. This time, too, it shifted the public sector oil companies' dollar demand directly to RBI reserves outside the open market and tightened liquidity. The central bank also hiked the rate of the Marginal Standing Facility – a window for overnight funds from the central bank in emergencies.  The rupee recovered from its low of 68.85 a dollar to around 62 within a few months – a 10 per cent appreciation – and foreign exchange reserves bounced back from $275 billion in mid-2013 to over $350 billion by early 2015.  In calendar year 2025, the rupee depreciated about 4.7 per cent, and in the current year, it hit an all-time low of 96.96 in May, representing a 7.3 per cent depreciation.  That prompted the RBI to announce a three-part dollar-rupee swap window for FNCR(B), external commercial borrowings (ECBs) and overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCBs). They opened on June 8 and the FCNR(B) window closed on August 31, a month before the scheduled closure because of strong response. Overall, this scheme raised $143.6 billion, including $132.98 billion through the FCNR(B) channel.  Even that could not arrest the slide of the local currency. In the last week of June, forex reserves were close to $667 billion. Riding the FCNR(B) flow, it rose to $785.7 billion in the first week of September. Since then, it has dropped to $726.3 bn (on October 9), falling almost $60 billion in six weeks.   Emulating the Chinese playbook, the RBI introduced a 20 per cent cash reserve requirement on any forex derivatives contract over $2 million. Called the Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), this forces banks to set aside a certain portion of their total exposure and keep it with the RBI.  In stage two, the ambit of FERR has been extended to cover non-deliverable contracts involving the rupee for non-resident customers for the purpose of hedging.  At the same time, the limit for foreign exchange derivative transactions for users without needing to establish the existence of underlying exposure has been cut down from $100 million to $5 million. This is also applicable to exchange-traded currency derivatives, which involve the rupee.  Also, banks cannot allow any corporate client to rebook a foreign exchange derivative contract that was cancelled. This is meant for both deliverable and non-derivable markets. Of course, the rollover of foreign exchange derivatives contracts on maturity will continue.  Finally, the RBI has opened a window to meet the dollar demand of public sector oil companies.  The objective behind all these measures is to curb speculation in the foreign exchange market.  After touching almost 97 to the dollar on October 9, the rupee has bounced back to 94.96 on October 16. Will the trend continue? Is there anything else the RBI can do?  Indeed, we need stability in the currency market but there is a cost attached to it. Since the banks will have to keep 20 per cent FERR with the RBI, they will not be able to use that money for giving loans. So, the cost will be passed on to corporate India. It will cut down speculation, discourage importers to over-hedge but have an impact on corporate balance sheets.  What we have been seeing is that exporters are not selling dollars earned in a hurry (as they feel the local currency will depreciate further) and importers are going overboard on hedging (for the same reason), leading to a gap in supply. It’s the so-called lead and lag phenomenon in the market.  It’s not a foreign exchange market problem alone. We have a situation where the rupee is undervalued but Indian assets are not seen as attractive. We will have to attract foreign money flow. How? That’s the key question. Could be by tax incentives, asset prices finding the right level, higher domestic demand, policy rate hike…  At the moment, there is just one choice before us: Let the rupee find its own level and allow that to happen in a calibrated way. The villain of the piece is the price of oil. If it comes down, problems will be solved, even if temporarily. For now, let’s not choke everything – the companies need to breathe.   Let’s end with a Chinese idiom: She ben qiu mo -- abandoning the root to chase the tip or branches. We need to address the root cause.  ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo       Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
