entry.title: Institutional stability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Institutional stabilityInstitutional stability

India needs timely appointments in higher education

premium

Prolonged vacancies in top academic positions raise concerns over faculty recruitment, research and institutional planning

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTSome of India’s premier higher-education institutions are facing a leadership vacuum, with 37 of the 155 Institutions of National Importance (23.9 per cent) operating under interim, acting or in-charge heads, additional-charge arrangements or extensions, according to a recent Hindustan Times analysis. The problem is particularly acute in central universities, where 20 of 48 institutions analysed have an interim leadership or extended tenures. Some vacancies persist despite posts being advertised months or even years earlier. This is more than an administrative inconvenience. Vice-chancellors and directors oversee faculty recruitment, academic programmes, budgets, infrastructure, and research partnerships. Prolonged uncertainty can delay decisions on new courses, the setting up of laboratories, and long-term financial commitments. Interim heads may also be reluctant to undertake major reforms when their authority is temporary. Additional-charge arrangements compound the problem by dividing the attention of senior academics between institutions. Hence, prolonged vacancies can put institutions in “standby mode”, weakening accountability and long-term planning.  The consequences are serious because leadership gaps coincide with wider capacity constraints in higher education. According to an analysis by PRS Legislative Research, 29 per cent of the sanctioned teaching posts in central universities were vacant as of December 2024. For professors, the vacancy rate stood at 56 per cent. These shortages place additional pressure on existing faculty. The appointment process also needs closer scrutiny. The analysis highlights cases in which selection procedures had begun well before the incumbent’s tenure ended, yet successors were not announced in time. Indira Gandhi National Tribal University, for instance, had functioned without a regular vice-chancellor for nearly 21 months, although the post had been advertised in June 2024 and re-advertised in March 2026. Such delays raise questions about administrative efficiency. Disputes over search committees and compliance with selection norms can further erode confidence in the process. Transparent, merit-based appointments are essential to protecting institutional credibility and autonomy.  The government should begin selection at least six months before a vacancy arises. It should establish binding timelines for screening applications, convening search committees and announcing appointments, with periodic public updates on progress. Such reporting would make delays visible and strengthen oversight without giving the government greater control over academic decisions. Committees should have clear selection criteria, independent members and safeguards against arbitrary interference. Interim appointments must be strictly time-bound, with extensions permitted only in exceptional circumstances and accompanied by a clear explanation. Institutions could also have contingency plans to ensure that essential academic and financial decisions continue during transitions. Strengthening leadership continuity and institutional autonomy is essential to improving research, teaching quality, and India’s global competitiveness in higher education. Timely leadership appointments are a basic requirement for that task. Leadership gaps and an inadequate strength of teaching staff, even in India’s premier institutions, could seriously undermine the country’s broader objective of achieving higher sustainable growth and becoming a developed country by 2047.     Topics : higher education vacancies governance Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Improved closing auction
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Improved closing auctionImproved closing auction

Sebi should aim to increase participation

premium

Securities and Exchange Board of India | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:13 PM ISTIt has been 10 weeks since the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) changed the way the stock markets end their trading day. It introduced the closing auction session (CAS) on August 3, with the idea of giving one efficient price for index funds, large institutional investors, and derivatives traders. But, instead, it led to problems — especially for derivatives traders, who decided to stay out of the market because of the unpredictability and volatility during the end session. A new circular dated October 15 addresses the issues and is in the right direction. It has delinked derivatives from the CAS close. The notional average daily derivatives turnover is more than 200 times that in cash. Retail investors account for about 40 per cent of the turnover in index options. The CAS was putting all these traders out of the system. The problems should be fixed in December.  The issue started when the indicative equilibrium prices in the CAS system fluctuated wildly as algo traders entered and cancelled orders, which led to volatility. The CAS settlement price is directly tied to expiring derivatives contracts, where traders had limited visibility of how the market would move. Thus, most derivatives traders and domestic funds stayed away from the market during the auction window. The bigger issue was that cash trading stopped at 3.15 pm while derivatives traded till 3.40 pm. The final value for the benchmark indices that came after the CAS was many a time far away from the closing price at 3.15 pm. Likewise for stocks that are part of the derivatives, or futures & options (F&O), segment.  The volumes handled in the auction are about 1 per cent of the daily cash turnover. The auction filled well on days when indices were rebalanced. For example, on the day of MSCI rebalance there were many buyers and sellers in the auction session and volumes were at 22 per cent of the entire trading day. But in normal days it lacked participants and sufficient volumes. In comparison, on the New York Stock Exchange, the CAS handles 12.43 per cent of daily volumes, and the same is 10 per cent for the Nasdaq. In such markets, it is hard for any single player to move the closing price because the CAS accounts for more than 10 per cent of the volumes. In India, the volumes are only 1 per cent and a small player can move stocks and thereby the index in the auction session and make money out of derivatives trades.  The new circular addresses most of these issues. From December 7, the expiry session goes back to the previous 25-year-old system of volume weighted average price (VWAP) while the daily closing price of underlying stocks will continue to be determined via CAS. Expiring index derivatives will stop trading at 3.30 pm or the same time as the cash markets. The auction will happen afterwards (3.30-3.40 pm) but stock derivatives will continue to trade until 3.45 pm.  This is a return to the old system but the auction stays and sets the official closing prices. But the link between derivatives and VWAP is restored. However, Sebi is yet to address how to bring in more passive funds to participate, improve the securities lending and borrowing mechanism (SLBM) or short selling, or separate auction order types that exist in the developed markets. A working stock-lending and short-selling market would let traders sell borrowed shares in an auction where buyers are bigger in numbers, narrowing the imbalances at the close. Thus, there is more to be done. Most importantly, fix stock lending and deepen the auction pool.     Topics : SEBI Indian stock market derivatives trading Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Sustaining progress
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Sustaining progressSustaining progress

India needs to create jobs to further reduce poverty

premium

India's poverty rate fell to 16.1% in 2023 from 57.7% in 2011, according to the World Bank, but creating better-paying jobs remains crucial to sustaining progress.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe World Bank’s October 2026 “Poverty and Equity Brief” showed that the share of Indians living below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day (2021 purchasing power parity) fell from 57.7 per cent in 2011 to 16.1 per cent in 2023, lifting 496 million people above this threshold. Extreme poverty, measured at $3 a day, declined to 2.6 per cent. The poverty rate at the $4.20 threshold is projected to fall further, from 14.2 per cent in 2026 to 12.1 per cent in 2028. However, nearly 80 per cent of Indians remained below the upper-middle-income poverty line of $8.30 a day in 2023. The challenge is to move above the upper threshold as quickly as possible.  Between 2017 and 2023, an additional 134 million received employment, with the increase being nearly twice the expansion of the working-age population. Yet the real earnings remained broadly unchanged, reflecting the concentration of new jobs in relatively low-productivity activities. The median earnings among the top 10 per cent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 per cent in 2023. The rise in youth unemployment from 14.6 per cent in the first quarter of FY26 to 15.9 per cent in the corresponding quarter of FY27 is another warning. All this needs to change. Further reduction in the poverty level and an increase in income levels in general can happen only through rapid expansion in employment opportunities.  The structure of employment in the country will be central to this effort. Agriculture accounted for 43 per cent of employment in 2025, while manufacturing’s share was only 12.1 per cent, according to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). This underscores the need to accelerate the shift towards more productive, better-paying non-farm jobs. Labour-intensive manufacturing, including textiles, apparel, footwear, food processing and electronics assembly, can absorb workers moving out of agriculture. Better infrastructure, industry-relevant skilling, easier access to credit, and predictable regulation can help firms expand and hire. Women’s participation is equally important. Although the female labour-force participation rate among those aged 15 and above was 40 per cent in 2025, as against 33.9 per cent in 2022, the urban rate remained much lower, at 27.7 per cent. The same rate among females in countries such as China and the United States is well over 50 per cent. Expanding women’s access to paid employment will require addressing barriers such as inadequate childcare facilities and unsafe transport, alongside more flexible work arrangements. An International Labour Organization study covering 82 countries estimated that every dollar invested in closing childcare gaps could generate $3.76 in global gross domestic product by 2035.  The geographical concentration of poverty makes state-level action crucial. Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal account for about 57 per cent of India’s poor population, according to the World Bank. Rural poverty, at 19.3 per cent, remains considerably higher than urban poverty, which is at 8.6 per cent. States with high poverty levels must compete to attract investment and generate stable, better-paying jobs. The Union government must focus more on these states to ensure equitable growth in the country.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Job creation in india Poverty in India World Bank report Poverty index

entry.title: Dropping barriers
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Dropping barriersDropping barriers

New Delhi must find ways to prise open China's markets

premium

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has flagged China's non-tariff barriers as a major obstacle to Indian exports, calling attention to the widening bilateral trade deficit.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 9:37 PM ISTSpeaking on the sidelines of the autumn meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok recently, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman highlighted concerns about India’s “exponentially growing” trade deficit with China. The minister pointed out that the problem in this case was not high tariffs but non-tariff barriers, which limited Indian companies’ market access in China. Phytosanitary rules, for example — safety regulations of various kinds — limited imports into China of Indian generic drugs, bovine products, and vegetables. For these sectors, among others, missing out on the large and growing Chinese market is a major problem. Meanwhile, Indian imports of Chinese goods, particularly in electronics, continue to grow at a rapid pace.  Ms Sitharaman’s statement has highlighted a problem that Indian trade policy may not currently be set up to address. India has entered into several free-trade agreements (FTAs) — and the one with New Zealand, for example, is coming into force today. These are important steps, in that they open up access to several vital markets, including the European Union and the United Kingdom. But Indian producers also need to expand their access to other countries, including emerging markets. China’s unwillingness to drop its non-tariff barriers is a major impediment in that effort.  To be sure, too much energy has been diverted over the past 18 months in dealing with the fallout of United States President Donald Trump’s attempt to derail global trade. In trying to minimise the effects of Mr Trump’s volatility on US-India trade, the government has sent conflicting signals on the progress of a bilateral deal with the US. It is unclear if talks are “plateauing”, as Ms Sitharaman has said, or if they are poised for a breakthrough, as some of her colleagues in the Cabinet have implied. But either way, the government cannot allow US-India relations to be its sole focus. The larger questions — such as reforming the multilateral trading system and ensuring that China plays a more responsible role within it — must also be made a priority.  Over the past year or so, India has attempted to reset its relations with China away from the lows plumbed after the clashes on the Line of Actual Control in mid-2020. Partly this was to ensure that Beijing placed no impediments in the way of the development of India’s high-end mobile-phone industry, which is dependent on supply chains that run through the mainland. This is also, as it happens, why concerns about increasing imports from China in the past couple of years should not be overstressed. If those imports are of intermediate inputs, to which value is added in Indian factories before being sold domestically or re-exported, then it is not necessarily a negative. The focus should, therefore, not be on the deficit or the scale of imports, but the failure to scale up exports to China. The finance minister is to be commended for making this point. It should be followed up by a comprehensive strategy that centres market access in New Delhi’s discussions with Beijing. It should be made clear that normalising the relationship will be dependent upon the Chinese leadership’s own choices about goods. It is not enough to drop tariffs. A broader acceptance that other non-tariff barriers must be lowered, alongside a step-by-step plan to accomplish that, should be a priority for India’s engagement with its northern neighbour.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment India China relations India china trade

entry.title: Building natural wealth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Building natural wealthBuilding natural wealth

Environmental accounts can inform policy decisions

premium

India's new environmental accounting strategy aims to measure the economic value of natural resources and ecosystem services to support sustainable development and better policy decisions.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTThe Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s (Mospi’s) new “Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026-30” is an attempt to measure the country’s natural resources and ecosystem services in a more systematic accounting framework. The rationale is straightforward. Natural resources form the backbone of economic activities, but their depletion and the services provided by ecosystems are not adequately reflected in conventional measures such as gross domestic product (GDP). The timing is important. As India pursues faster growth amid increasing pressure on land and water, policymakers need to know not only how much the economy produces, but also what it is consuming from its natural-resource base. The strategy follows the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) and builds on Mospi’s work since 2018. The pollination account can illustrate why this matters. Mospi estimates the value of pollination services at ₹2.66 trillion in 2021-22, up from ₹1.15 trillion in 2012-13, equivalent to roughly 8-10 per cent of crop output. Conventional agricultural accounts capture the value of the crop, but not the ecosystem service that contributes to producing it. Making such a contribution visible can strengthen the economic case for protecting pollinators, supporting beekeeping and designing pollinator-friendly agricultural policies. The same logic applies to water accounts, which can help policymakers assess resource use and groundwater stress, and also to mineral accounts, which can track extraction, depletion and discoveries.  The strategy also has a wider development role. Mospi estimates that environmental accounts can support the assessment of about 40 global indicators across nine Sustainable Development Goals. The new road map expands the coverage to carbon stocks, biodiversity and environment-related economic activities, potentially making environmental information more useful for decisions extending well beyond the environment ministry. International experience shows what such accounting can achieve. The United Kingdom (UK) natural-capital accounts estimated the annual value of ecosystem services at £41 billion in 2023, while the asset value of natural capital was estimated at £1.6 trillion. Such estimates bring nature into discussions of national wealth rather than treating it only as an environmental concern.  But measurement is only the first hurdle. Implementation is the harder test. India has undertaken environmental-accounting studies at state level for years, but differences in concepts, definitions, and methods have prevented these efforts from being aggregated into a consistent national picture. Only 18 states and Union Territories have so far constituted inter-departmental groups on environmental accounting, while Mospi itself identifies a shortage of expertise in the SEEA framework. The next five years should, therefore, focus less on adding accounts for their own sake and more on making them comparable, timely and usable. Common definitions, interoperable state databases, spatially consistent data, and trained officials are necessary. Most importantly, the accounts must enter the decision-making process — from groundwater allocation and mining permits to land-use planning and forest restoration. The real success of the 2026-30 strategy will not be the number of accounts published but whether the depletion of natural wealth can be arrested for sustainable development.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Natural resources Sustainable Development Goals

entry.title: Waiving double standards
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Waiving double standardsWaiving double standards

Mr Trump discovers merits of national interest

premium

US President Donald Trump's decision to temporarily waive sanctions on Russian oil imports has raised questions over Washington's policy consistency and its commitment to Ukraine | Photo: White House

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:45 PM ISTUnited States (US) President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russian imports under a congressional law must be seen as a relief for India both in terms of its oil-import policy and for concluding the long-awaited trade deal, which had stalled mainly on this account as well as Section 301 investigations. On a broader canvas, the 60-day waiver demonstrates the Trump regime’s double standards, ratchets up strategic uncertainty over US support for ally Ukraine in its war against Russia, and generally raises global misgivings about US reliability as an ally.  The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026, gave the President the powers to impose 100 per cent tariffs on major Russian oil buyers such as India and China, to deprive Moscow of revenue to finance its war against Ukraine. When the war broke out in February 2022, and the West drew down Russian oil and gas purchases in solidarity with Ukraine, India chose to accept the deep discounts offered by a traditional ally. This move was excoriated by Mr Trump, who imposed an additional punitive 25 per cent tariff on Indian imports in August 2025, later lifted following an interim trade framework in February this year. India’s imports of Russian oil rose steadily from about 2 per cent of all its purchase of crude oil to almost 50 per cent, as New Delhi sought to parry sharply rising global oil prices as a result of Western sanctions. Despite the fulminations from the White House, the validity of this approach, driven by national interests, was underlined by the fact that the US continued to import uranium from Russia despite the war.  This latest waiver, driven by electoral considerations ahead of November mid-term polls and signed a day before the 30-day enforcement deadline, has undermined even further the logical tenability of US objections to India’s imports of Russian oil. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following US-Israel attacks on Iran has exerted upward pressure on prices of oil products, and like others, the American people are feeling the pinch. Diesel prices have risen 66-68 per cent over the year, driving up prices all round. The grounds for the waiver, enabled by Section 115 of the Lindsey Graham Act, were prepared on October 9, when the US Treasury issued a temporary licence allowing the sale and import of Russian diesel into the global market until April 7, 2027.  The agreement with Russia will immediately provide the US 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes subsequently. Russia will also release 3 million tonnes, depending on the state of its refineries (some of which were recently attacked by Ukraine).  This remarkable geostrategic pivot is also driven by Mr Trump’s tensions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has accused the US administration of scaling back military support and intelligence sharing. Delays in supplying promised Patriot missiles and deteriorating Starlink satellite services, which have impacted drone performance and battlefield communications, have been notable setbacks for Ukraine of late. As US allies add their voice to lawmakers, including some Republicans, on the amorality of the latest waiver, it is ironic that Mr Trump should offer the national-interest counter-argument — which he emphatically rejected in India’s case a year ago.   Topics : Donald Trump BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Russia US Russia Russia Ukraine Conflict

entry.title: Best of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished away
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished awayBest of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished away

Today's editorials and columns examine the trade-offs shaping India's economic policies, from China trade and poverty reduction to rupee management and the hidden costs of clean energy

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTPolicy choices rarely come without a bill. Opening markets can increase opportunity but also exposure. Reducing poverty may leave the hardest pockets of deprivation behind. Supporting one macroeconomic objective can make another harder to achieve. Defending a currency may buy stability while creating distortions elsewhere. Even clean energy carries environmental and geopolitical costs. The difficult part of policymaking is not finding benefits; it is deciding which costs are worth bearing, who should bear them, and how they can be contained. Our first editorial today, “Dropping barriers”, looks at India’s economic engagement with China. New Delhi has reason to seek better access to Chinese markets and press Beijing to dismantle tariff and non-tariff barriers that disadvantage Indian exporters. Greater access could help narrow the trade imbalance and create opportunities for Indian firms. But closer engagement cannot ignore strategic vulnerability or the competitive pressure created by China’s industrial strength. India must therefore pursue market access without allowing economic dependence to deepen. Openness can create gains, but only if it is accompanied by stronger domestic competitiveness and a clear-eyed assessment of risk. The second editorial, “Sustaining progress”, turns to poverty reduction. World Bank estimates suggest India has made significant progress, but aggregate improvement can obscure those who remain difficult to reach. Poverty is increasingly concentrated in certain states, regions and social groups, while employment quality and income security remain critical. The next stage is harder than the last. Sustaining the gains will require more jobs, better targeting and sharper attention to areas that have not benefited equally from growth. Ananth Narayan’s column, “Confronting economic trade-offs”, makes the theme more explicit. Monetary and financial policy involves objectives that can pull in different directions. Interest rates, liquidity, inflation, the exchange rate, fiscal conditions and capital flows cannot all be optimised independently. A measure that eases one pressure can intensify another. The challenge for policymakers is not to eliminate trade-offs, which is impossible, but to acknowledge them, rank priorities and communicate those choices clearly. Rajeswari Sengupta’s column, “RBI’s rupee fix: What is it solving?”, asks whether recent efforts to support the rupee are aimed at the right problem. Measures that ease immediate pressure on the currency may provide temporary stability, but they cannot substitute for stronger underlying capital flows and external-sector fundamentals. If the diagnosis is wrong, the cure can impose new costs without resolving the original weakness. “Dirty truths behind clean energy”, Prosenjit Datta’s review of Nicolas Niarchos’ The Elements of Power, exposes the trade-offs embedded in the energy transition itself. Batteries, solar equipment and electric vehicles promise lower carbon emissions, but depend on large-scale extraction of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other minerals, creating environmental, social and geopolitical risks of their own. There are few costless choices, these pieces reveal. Good policy begins when the trade-offs are made visible rather than wished away.

entry.title: Best of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also exists
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Best of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also existsBest of Business Standard Opinion: What sits outside the frame also exists

What makes these risks dangerous is not only their existence, but the ease with which institutions can ignore them when they are difficult to measure, explain or fit into established categories

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTSome risks are obvious. Others sit outside the frame: a national interest concealed behind universal rules, environmental depletion missing from economic accounts, currency exposure left unhedged, financial risk buried in product structure, or an illness whose cause remains disputed. What makes these risks dangerous is not only their existence, but the ease with which institutions can ignore them when they are difficult to measure, explain or fit into established categories. Our first editorial today, “Waiving double standards”, looks at the US’ sanctions policy towards Russian oil. Washington has repeatedly argued for strict limits on countries buying Russian crude oil, yet it has also made exceptions when its own strategic or economic interests are involved. The editorial argues that this selective application weakens the policy’s credibility. The hidden variable is national interest: what is presented as a universal rule is often shaped by the calculations of the country enforcing it. For India, that makes it important to respond — not only to the stated principle but also to the interests driving it.  The second editorial, “Building natural wealth”, turns to what conventional economic measurement leaves out. GDP can record production and income while missing the depletion of forests, water, minerals and other natural assets. Environmental accounts attempt to correct that blind spot by treating natural resources as part of the country’s wealth. The larger point: if depletion is not measured, it can easily be mistaken for growth. Bringing natural capital into public accounting would allow policymakers to see the economic cost of consuming assets that may take decades, or longer, to restore. Mihir S Sharma’s column, “Let the people hedge”, applies the same idea to forex risk. Indians have genuine exposure to overseas currencies through education, travel, investments and other transactions. Yet policy remains restrictive about allowing individuals to hedge those exposures freely. The risk does not disappear because the hedge is unavailable. It simply remains with the individual. Sharma argues that a more mature forex framework should recognise the exposure people already carry and allow them the tools to manage it. Debashis Basu’s column, “AT-1 bonds: The bigger lessons”, shows how hidden risk can become visible only after damage is done. Additional Tier-I bonds contain loss-absorption features that many investors may not have fully understood. The Yes Bank episode exposed weaknesses in disclosure, suitability and regulation. Complex financial products are not inherently problematic, but risks buried in technical language or sold to unsuitable investors can create a false sense of safety. “The mystery of the ‘Havana Syndrome’”, Nicolas Niarchos’ review of Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados’ The Havana Syndrome, looks at uncertainty itself. Years after American officials reported mysterious illnesses, the evidence around their cause remains contested. The difficulty lies in responding to experiences that are real to those affected while the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. What cannot be easily seen or measured still has consequences, these pieces show. Often, the greater danger lies in pretending that what sits outside the frame does not exist.Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Consumer Protection: Don't risk renewal by handing cheque to agent
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Consumer Protection: Don't risk renewal by handing cheque to agentConsumer Protection: Don't risk renewal by handing cheque to agent

The Supreme Court held that an agent had neither express nor implied authority to receive premiums on the insurer's behalf, and hence upheld the repudiation of claims

premium

Jehangir B Gai New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:38 PM ISTThe premium had been paid to the agent well before the fatal accident. For Harshad J Shah’s widow, that was reason enough to expect the insurer to honour her claims. The insurer disagreed. The money had not reached it on time, and the policies had lapsed, it contended.  The dispute, which went all the way to the Supreme Court, holds a lesson for policyholders who leave renewal payments to their agents. Handing over the money may feel like the job is done. But if the agent does not deposit it, the policyholder could lose cover.  Dependence has consequences  Agents commonly collect renewal premiums as part of their service. Customers often see this as the agent’s duty. After all, the agent earns a commission when the policy is renewed. It may seem a legitimate expectation, but it leaves a crucial question unanswered: Who bears the loss if the premium never reaches the insurer?  An agent may simply forget to deposit the money or become caught up in a personal problem. In rare instances, an agent may collude with the insurer to deliberately let a policy lapse when a high claims ratio makes it economically unviable. Whatever the reason for the lapse, the policyholder suffers.  Courts have delivered conflicting judgments on whether an insurer must renew a policy when its agent has collected the premium. This crucial issue has been put to rest by the Supreme Court in Harshad J Shah and Anr v Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC).  Shah had taken four policies of ₹25,000 each from LIC, with premiums payable half-yearly. One instalment did not reach the insurer by the due date. Shah subsequently died in an accident. His widow, the nominee under the policies, lodged claims. LIC repudiated them on the ground that the policies had lapsed on account of non-payment of the premium on time.  Shah’s widow approached the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Maharashtra State Commission) with a consumer complaint. She contended that the claim should  be settled, as the premium had been paid to the agent much before her husband’s fatal accident. LIC’s defence turned on the agent’s authority. Its agents, it argued, are not authorised to collect premiums on its behalf. Paying an agent therefore does not amount to paying the insurer. The dispute ultimately reached the Supreme Court.  The apex court examined the Life Insurance Corporation of India (Agents) Regulations, 1972. Regulation 8(4), it noted, bars an agent from collecting money or accepting any risk on behalf of the insurer. The letter of engagement issued to an agent or broker also incorporates this condition.  The court held that an agent had neither express nor implied authority to receive premiums on the insurer’s behalf. It upheld the repudiation of the claims and concluded that LIC was not liable to settle them.  Ensure payment reaches insurer  The practical lesson is straightforward. Pay renewal premiums directly to the insurer and ensure the money reaches it on time. You can pay online or send a cheque by registered post or speed post.  If you use a cheque, what matters is when the insurer receives it, regardless of when it presents or encashes it. A cheque that arrives before the policy expires and is subsequently encashed maintains the continuity of the policy. Handing over the renewal payment to an agent could leave you without the protection you thought you had paid for.

entry.title: 12 questions for Rahul
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / 12 questions for Rahul12 questions for Rahul

What will Rahul Gandhi do differently from Modi/BJP if elected? Here's a list of a dozen short questions

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi faces the challenge of building a credible policy alternative to Prime Minister Narendra Modi ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections, beyond relying on political protests and criticism of the government.(Photo:PTI)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 9:46 AM ISTIf Rahul Gandhi is the flavour of the political season for adversaries and fans alike, two interesting trends dominate all talk over his future. Both are contradictory. On the one hand, it’s quite remarkable that there’s disagreement between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his mass base over Rahul’s future potential. On the other hand, Rahul and his base are in complete agreement on this subject. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) followers are dismissive of Rahul. For them, he’s “Pappu”, or an object of derision. Often enough, even senior BJP leaders boast that he’s no threat but their biggest strength. Mr Modi, however, has always held the opposite view. He sees Rahul, and the Gandhis, as the only potential threat.  That’s why his campaigns are so fixated on Rahul. Even in a state election where the Congress hardly counts, Mr Modi targets him. This week, he also fielded Union Home Minister and BJP “Kautilya” Amit Shah to launch a vicious attack on Rahul. While the base may laugh it away, BJP seniors know who the real threat is. That’s the rare contradiction between the leader and the base. For the Congress, Rahul and his base are unanimous in believing that power is his for the taking, if only elections were fair. Implicit in this is the insinuation that all elections were stolen by the BJP 2019 onwards. First, by “mass-fixing” of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), and now with a combination of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and his SIR. Just fix these and the next election is yours.

Also Read

 Unlike their devoted base, Mr Modi and Mr Shah are realistic about Rahul because they know their politics. Rahul’s followers and Mr Modi agree on one thing, and they’re both right that however consistently Rahul may have faltered in the past, the Congress under him poses the only credible challenge to the BJP. See it this way. From its lowest Lok Sabha tally of 44 seats in 2014 through 52 in 2019 to 99 in 2024, the Congress vote share has been steady in the 19-21 per cent range. That’s one in five Indians instinctively voting for the “hand” symbol. Looking at data from 1996 through 2009, the BJP floated within the 25 per cent ballpark. That’s one in four voters. It was the coalition era. Mr Modi changed that equation in 2014. The BJP has floated in the 37-40 per cent range since. A jump of 12-15 percentage points over the baseline is phenomenal and devastating in a multi-party system. We can safely call this top-up the Modi vote. It’s unrealistic to imagine Rahul taking the Congress vote share to 37 per cent in the foreseeable future. But, if he simply adds another 5-6 per cent to his core vote, national politics changes. He’s been routinely losing 9 out of 10 direct fights against the BJP. You can then presume that most of this vote will come from the BJP in regions it routinely sweeps. The 2024 election was a limited coalition exception. As the Opposition vote consolidated, BJP’s strike rate declined. It won only 7 out of every 10 direct contests against the Congress. A BJP at 32 per cent will still dominate, but its Lok Sabha numbers could fall to low-200s or even below that. It may still form a government, but it will be a genuine National Democratic Alliance coalition, with all the attendant leadership complications. That’s the threat Mr Modi and Mr Shah have never taken lightly. They don’t believe Rahul is their best asset in the Opposition. They know that the Congress, with its one-in-five vote base, is their only challenger. And the Congress, like it or not, can’t stay intact without the Gandhis. Now, the key point: Where does this take Rahul? At this time, he’s totally focused on building the “street” against Mr Modi. He’s willing to partner anybody, from mostly apolitical CJP to hard-Left All India Students’ Association, from Abhijeet Dipke to Neha Bora. Having been through the school of hard knocks since he joined politics in 2004, Rahul should know that political change in India is brought about either by those who win an election, or combine with others to defeat an incumbent. A “regime change” on the streets is an empty hard-Left fantasy because they can never win an election. The combined might of Jayaprakash Narayan (Navnirman Andolan) and George Fernandes (Railway Strike), backed by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and Lohiaite street power and armed with that Allahabad High Court order, couldn’t topple Indira Gandhi. They had to wait for the 1977 election. In 2010-12, a dead-in-the-water United Progressive Alliance wasn’t thrown out by the Anna movement and RSS/BJP. It took the 2014 election to settle the issue. The next general election in 2029 will mark 25 years in politics for Rahul. He will still be only 59, young by the standards of Indian politics. But presuming that the Congress and the BJP retain their ideologically frozen vote, Mr Modi’s add-on voters won’t shift to Rahul out of boredom. He has to offer them a better, constructive, optimistic proposition. What will he do differently from Modi/BJP if elected? Let me list just a dozen short questions: 
  • How would he want Election Commissioners to be picked and the impartiality of Election Commission of India restored? Return to the Congress/UPA era isn’t inspiring. His late father had tried in 1989 to weaken the EC by making it a three-member body. Further, how will he ensure that non-citizens (those the BJP has labelled ghuspethiyas) don’t become voters?
  • The same for the judiciary, CBI and the other key agencies.
  • How will he handle a Trump-like challenge? How will his policy towards the United States be any different?
  • What’s his plan to deal with the Chinese? How will his treatment of Pakistan and terrorism emanating from there be different? Softer than Modi’s, or harder?
  • How will his approach to West Asia and Israel differ from Modi’s?
  • What’s his vision for managing India’s chronic and crippling triple-shortage of energy, capital and gold? We can add AI/software services to this now. How will he make India a magnet for investors?
  • Chhatron ki Goonj is resonating. But how will he create more jobs? Further, for the less educated, will he restore MGNREGA, or introduce a “new, improved” version? Will he continue giving away free food grains?
  • Is caste Census still his idea of social justice? How will it create more jobs? Revanth Reddy doesn’t know what to do with his caste Census. Will he ask D K Shivakumar to at least release his caste Census data?
  • What changes does he plan for the education system to end corruption and profiteering, improve the quality of education, and make the young more employable?
  • He says he isn’t anti-business or anti-capital. He just wants no monopoly and a level playing field. How will he ensure that? What’s his concept of economic reform?
  • Since he and his “secular” partners complain that the minorities are marginalised, how would he mainstream them?
  • And finally, who is, or will be on his team?
 To look like a credible challenger and not just a street-fighter, Rahul needs to answer these questions and offer voters in the “middle” new ideas. Mr Modi started promising “Achche Din” by late 2012. At about the same distance from 2029, what’s Rahul promising? If he were to think out of the box, he could set up a UK-style shadow Cabinet. His “ministers” could then start answering these questions in their respective domains. Of course, if I were to be only part facetious, it could unleash mighty infighting even for these non-jobs. Whatever Rahul Gandhi chooses, he can’t go into 2029 again riding on his ecosystem’s clamour over Modi’s “falling” popularity. That has failed thrice already.

Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: India must bring its brightest minds home, like China didBest of Opinion: India must bring its brightest minds home, like China did

Today's columns examine India's failure to use its skilled diaspora, succession challenges in family businesses, Rahul Gandhi's political strategy, and resistance to resource-intensive data centres

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  Shyam Saran contrasts China’s success in building scientific and technological capabilities with India’s failure to harness its skilled diaspora. Deng Xiaoping’s reforms combined investment in education and research with technology transfers, overseas study and collaboration between foreign experts and Chinese institutions. India, by contrast, often fails to provide returning professionals with adequate research facilities or a welcoming institutional environment. Saran argues that promoting skilled migration while struggling to create meaningful domestic employment reflects a policy failure. With artificial intelligence becoming strategically crucial, he urges India to expand its existing centres of excellence and attract overseas talent to strengthen its scientific and technological capabilities.  Family-owned businesses face a persistent tension between cultural preferences for family leadership and the need to appoint the most competent executives. Succession requires clear distinctions between ownership, governance and management, alongside rigorous assessment and mentoring of potential heirs. R Gopalakrishnan recommends succession committees comprising family members and independent directors, with successors tested through challenging assignments and professional chief executives appropriately recognised. Brazil’s JBS offers an example: after its founder’s sons presided over rapid expansion and a corruption scandal, professional CEO Gilberto Tomazoni led the company for eight years before handing over to the founder’s grandson, who had undergone extensive grooming. Rahul Gandhi’s political prospects present a paradox: while BJP supporters dismiss him, Narendra Modi and Amit Shah treat the Congress leader as a serious challenger. The Congress retains a substantial vote base, and Shekhar Gupta argues that even a modest increase could significantly alter parliamentary arithmetic. But street mobilisation and allegations of electoral manipulation cannot substitute for a constructive alternative. With 2029 approaching, Gupta challenges Rahul to spell out policies on institutions, foreign affairs, jobs, caste, education, economic reform and minority inclusion. He might consider adopting a UK-style shadow cabinet to develop credible alternatives, given that criticism of Modi alone will not suffice. Growing resistance to data centres reflects their heavy consumption of power and water, limited job creation and concerns over privacy and political favouritism. Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex facilities in Russia also highlight their vulnerability and potential role in hosting malicious online activity. In the US, opposition has become bipartisan, with some states considering moratoriums, while European projects face delays. Devangshu Datta cautions that India, despite the opportunity to attract investments displaced from Western markets, faces tighter resource constraints. Local resistance could grow if communities see few benefits, and might even limit losses if the AI investment boom collapses.
